name: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
title: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
answer: This page covers the fiduciary duties of corporate directors when their companies adopt or rely on artificial intelligence, including the duty of care, the duty of loyalty, and the obligation to oversee material risks. It addresses how boards evaluate AI use cases, vendor relationships, and internal model governance against evolving legal standards. The scope also includes monitoring active AI litigation, case law precedents, and state and federal regulatory activity that can shape director liability. It is written for corporate secretaries, general counsel, and board members who need to understand AI risk without being machine learning engineers.

sections.body: This page covers the fiduciary duties of corporate directors when their companies adopt or rely on artificial intelligence, including the duty of care, the duty of loyalty, and the obligation to oversee material risks. It addresses how boards evaluate AI use cases, vendor relationships, and internal model governance against evolving legal standards. The scope also includes monitoring active AI litigation, case law precedents, and state and federal regulatory activity that can shape director liability. It is written for corporate secretaries, general counsel, and board members who need to understand AI risk without being machine learning engineers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on continuously updated repositories of AI-related legal and regulatory information, including the site's tracking of 142 active AI lawsuits, 29 AI case law precedents, 210 compliance and regulation pages, and 6895 state AI bills. These sources allow board advisors to compare a company's AI practices against current litigation theories and legislative requirements. The infrastructure also includes glossaries and tool directories that help nontechnical directors understand the systems under review. No single software platform is required; the core resource is the curated, cross-referenced legal database.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Board advisory work typically begins with an inventory of the company's AI systems, their data sources, and the decisions they support or automate. Advisors then map each system to the board's oversight duties, identifying where a failure could cause financial, reputational, or legal harm. The method includes reviewing board minutes, committee charters, and management reports to assess whether AI risk is being escalated properly. Advisors also track litigation and enforcement actions to update risk assessments as legal theories evolve. The output is usually a board briefing or a risk register, not a technical model audit.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Fiduciary risk in AI arises mainly from failures of oversight, disclosure, and conflict management. Directors can face derivative claims if they ignore repeated warnings about AI harms or if they approve AI vendor contracts without reviewing data provenance and model limitations. Rights and responsibilities also turn on the provenance of training data and the auditability of model decisions, because boards must be able to show that they made informed choices. The site's tracking of 92 intellectual property lawsuits among 142 active AI lawsuits highlights a recurring source of board-level exposure. Governance practice therefore focuses on documenting the board's inquiry and the reasons for its decisions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Board oversight of AI is moving from voluntary best practice to a formal part of enterprise risk management, driven by state law fragmentation and increasing derivative litigation. The 6895 state AI bills tracked on this site suggest that directors will face a patchwork of disclosure and risk assessment duties rather than a single federal standard. Expect more board committees to add AI risk to audit or risk committee charters, and more shareholder proposals asking for AI transparency reports. As case law develops, the standard for what a careful director must know about AI will likely rise, pushing boards toward documented, repeatable oversight processes.
